intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: The vault before you holds the history of computer vision, scattered across sealed rooms.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: Each room opens when you've pieced its fragment of the timeline back together.

rooms.title: The Timeline Room
rooms.description: A dusty corkboard pinned with photographs of cat brains, block shapes, and a camera lens, waiting to be strung in order.

rooms.title: The Sketching Room
rooms.description: Four easels hold sketches of a scene at increasing levels of detail, beside shelves stuffed with labeled photo bins.

rooms.title: The Claims Room
rooms.description: A chalkboard covered in bold statements about neural networks, some underlined in red, waiting to be judged true or false.

boss.mechanicReason: The final lock asks you to rebuild the full historical sequence spanning every room's discovery.

item.prompt: The vault door wants the entire history of computer vision laid out from earliest to latest.

steps.text: Hubel & Wiesel study how simple, complex, and hypercomplex brain cells respond to light orientation and movement.
Larry Roberts builds the 'Block World' program, extracting feature points from simple shapes.
David Marr proposes stages of visual representation, from perceived intensities to a 3-D model.
Viola & Jones develop a practical face detection algorithm.
Convolutional Neural Networks become an important tool for object recognition.

item.why: Each milestone carries its own year or decade, placing neuroscience research first, then early vision programs, then Marr's theory, then face detection, then the rise of CNNs.

sourceRefs.quote: Stages of Visual Representation, David Marr, 1970s
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have become an important tool for object recognition

hints: Start with brain cells, end with the modern tool that 'was not invented overnight.'

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The vault seal breaks. You have rebuilt a century of seeing machines, piece by piece.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: This wing holds the course itself, locked behind its own syllabus.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: Understand its shape, its grading, and its rules to find the way out.

rooms.title: The Task Board Room
rooms.description: A corkboard of labeled photographs — detection boxes, captions, action tags — sorted into two overlapping lists.

rooms.title: The Scope Room
rooms.description: A wall of banners proclaiming the course's ambitions, some overreaching, waiting to be swiped true or false.

rooms.title: The Grading Room
rooms.description: A ledger of percentages and a calendar of late days sits on a desk, demanding both memorization and careful reasoning.

boss.mechanicReason: The final lock requires reasoning about how the grading components interact, not just recalling each weight alone.

item.scenario: A student misses the midterm entirely, due to illness, but still plans to submit all problem sets and the final course project.
item.prompt: Based on the grading breakdown, which statement is best supported?

options.text: If a student misses the midterm entirely, at most 85% of the final grade remains achievable.
options.feedback: Correct: the midterm is worth 15%, so losing it caps the remaining achievable grade at 85%.

options.text: A student can still earn full marks even without submitting the final course project.
options.feedback: Incorrect: the Final Course Project is worth 40% of the grade, so skipping it prevents full marks.

options.text: The midterm counts for the same weight as the three problem sets combined.
options.feedback: Incorrect: the three problem sets combined are worth 45%, while the midterm alone is only 15%.

hints: Add up what the midterm is worth, then subtract it from 100% to see the ceiling.

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The syllabus wing unlocks. You now know the course as well as its grading policy knows you.
